Image-Based Deep Learning for Volatility
Forecasting: A CNN–HAR Fusion Approach Using
Intraday Returns
Niklas Betz∗
Thomas L.A. Heil†
Franziska J. Peter‡
Abstract
We forecast next-day realized volatility using intraday return images
processed by convolutional neural networks (CNNs). Returns are encoded
as sign-aware “waterfall” images, allowing the models to capture nonlinear
and asymmetric intraday dynamics.
We propose a hybrid CNN–fusion
framework that combines daily, weekly, and monthly CNN predictions within
a HAR-style structure. Using minute-level data for 30 Dow Jones stocks
(2005–2023), the models outperform HAR and GARCH benchmarks under
MSE and QLIKE. Diebold–Mariano tests confirm significant gains, while
Model Confidence Set results indicate a trade-off between accuracy and

firm significant gains, while
Model Confidence Set results indicate a trade-off between accuracy and
robustness. Explainable AI analysis shows that negative returns receive
greater importance and that models shift attention toward short horizons
in high-volatility periods. These findings highlight the value of image-based
deep learning for volatility forecasting.
Keywords: Volatility forecasting; Convolutional neural networks; Intraday returns;
Realized volatility; Image-based learning; HAR model; Explainable AI

Introduction
Financial volatility plays a critical role in determining security valuation, investment
strategies, risk management, and even shaping monetary policy. Consequently,
developing accurate models for volatility forecasting has attracted substantial
interest from both academics and practitioners alike.
One widely recognized
approach is the Heterogeneous Autoregressive (HAR) model, introduced by Corsi
(2009), which has become a benchmark in contemporary finance literature for
volatility prediction. Relying on realized volatility (RV) derived from high-frequency
data (Andersen and Ter¨asvirta, 2009, Barndorff-Nielsen and Shephard, 2002),
the HAR model offers a parsimonious but effective framework that captures the
persistent and multi-scale nature of daily volatility.
However,

persistent and multi-scale nature of daily volatility.
However, since the HAR model is specified as a linear forecasting combination
based on aggregation of squared intraday returns as realized volatility measures,
potentially informative dynamics contained in high-frequency return data are not
directly accessible within this forecasting model, yet, nonlinear patterns, temporal
clustering, and asymmetries in intraday returns could be relevant for predicting
future volatility. Therefore, in this study, we address this limitation by employing
convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to explicitly allow high-frequency information
to enter the volatility forecasting framework. In financial applications, CNNs have
already demonstrated strong performance in

recasting framework. In financial applications, CNNs have
already demonstrated strong performance in modeling complex intraday dynamics
and nonlinear dependencies (Jiang et al., 2023; Kristjanpoller and Minutolo, 2015;
Miura et al., 2019; Rahimikia and Poon, 2020; Reisenhofer et al., 2022; Sezer and
Ozbayoglu, 2018; Zhang et al., 2023; Zhu et al., 2023).
More broadly, the literature has evolved along two complementary strands. In
the finance-oriented literature, deep learning models have been applied to realized
volatility forecasting, often focusing on improving predictive accuracy relative to

 https://ssrn.com/abstract=4584108

traditional benchmarks. In parallel, the machine learning and computer science
literature has developed increasingly sophisticated neural architectures, including
hybrid models such as CEEMDAN-LSTM, reinforcement learning-based approaches,
and recent deep forecasting frameworks (Lin et al., 2022; Souto and Moradi, 2024;
Yu et al., 2023), as well as CNN-based volatility prediction in related financial
domains (Vidal and Kristjanpoller, 2020).
Despite these advances, prior work typically emphasizes either predictive performance or model architecture, with limited attention to economically interpretable
frameworks based on image representations. We address this gap by combining
sign-aware intraday return images with a multi-horizon forecasting structure that
preserves the economic intuition

raday return images with a multi-horizon forecasting structure that
preserves the economic intuition of the HAR model while exploiting the nonlinear
feature extraction capabilities of CNNs. This joint integration of image-based
inputs, multi-horizon modeling, and explicit explainability has received relatively
limited attention in the volatility forecasting literature.
Specifically, we encode high-frequency stock returns as two-dimensional inputs
and train three horizon-specific CNN models corresponding to daily, weekly, and
monthly information sets. Each network learns a nonlinear predictor of nextday realized volatility directly from intraday data. The resulting horizon-level
predictions are subsequently combined through a linear fusion layer inspired by
the additive multi-horizon

tions are subsequently combined through a linear fusion layer inspired by
the additive multi-horizon structure of the HAR model.
This paper makes three main contributions. First, we introduce an image-based
representation of intraday returns that preserves temporal structure and sign
information, enabling CNNs to capture nonlinear and asymmetric patterns. Second,
we propose a multi-horizon CNN–fusion architecture that mirrors the HAR structure
while allowing flexible, data-driven feature learning. Third, we provide a combined
evaluation and explainability analysis using out-of-sample tests, gradient-based

 https://ssrn.com/abstract=4584108

attribution, and counterfactual experiments, offering insights into the drivers of
volatility forecasts.
The remainder of this paper is structured as follows. Section 2 introduces the benchmark HAR model, the CNN-based models, the time-series image transformation,
and CNN architecture. Section 3 discusses the dataset, while sections 4 presents the
volatility prediction results including statistical tests for the prediction accuracy.
Section 5 provides the explainable AI analysis. Finally, Section 6 concludes the
paper.

CNN-based volatility prediction approach, the intraday image generation process,
and the CNN architecture.

2.3
CNN Architecture for Realized Volatility Prediction
We employ separate CNNs for the daily, weekly, and monthly inputs. Each network
processes images of size 380 × 380 with three color channels. The architecture
consists of three convolutional layers, which use a stride of two. Each convolutional
layer is followed by max-pooling, to progressively extract and downsample spatial
features. The resulting feature maps are passed to a fully connected layer with
dropout regularization to mitigate overfitting. The final dense

ssed to a fully connected layer with
dropout regularization to mitigate overfitting. The final dense layer contains 500
neurons and produces the volatility prediction. Figure 3 illustrates the complete
architecture.

Figure 3: Final CNN model
Hyperparameters are selected via grid search. The optimal configuration uses an
initial learning rate of 10−4 with the Adam optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014), a
batch size of 8, and convolutional layers with 16, 32, and 64 filters, respectively. All
convolutional layers use 3 × 3 kernels and ReLU activation functions (Goodfellow
et al., 2016). To account for training stochasticity, we estimate ensembles of CNNs
at each horizon and average their forecasts (Gu et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2023).
Based on validation RMSE, each network is trained for twenty epochs.
The fusion model is trained using a two-stage procedure. First, separate CNNs
are estimated for each horizon (daily, weekly, and monthly) as indicated above. In

a second stage, these pretrained networks are combined through a linear fusion
layer that takes their individual predictions as inputs. The entire model, including
both the CNN components and the fusion layer, is then jointly fine-tuned for an

Realized Volatility Prediction Results
After fitting all models on the training sample, we evaluate out-of-sample performance on the test dataset along three dimensions: (i) forecast dynamics, (ii)
point-forecast accuracy under MSE and QLIKE, and (iii) statistical significance.
MSE provides a scale-dependent measure of forecast accuracy, whereas QLIKE is
widely used in volatility forecasting due to its robustness to measurement error in
realized volatility. In addition, QLIKE imposes an asymmetric loss that penalizes
underprediction of volatility more strongly than overprediction.

4.4
Model Confidence Set Analysis
We complement the DM results with a Model Confidence Set (MCS) procedure
following Hansen et al., 2011, which evaluates forecast robustness under dependence
in loss differentials. The MCS identifies a subset of models that are statistically
indistinguishable from the best-performing model at

tifies a subset of models that are statistically
indistinguishable from the best-performing model at a given confidence level,
based on sequential elimination of inferior models, thereby accounting for multiple
comparisons and avoiding spurious rejections.

 https://ssrn.com/abstract=4584108

Inference is based on the Tmax statistic using a block bootstrap (B = 3000, block
length 10) at the 5% confidence level. The bootstrap procedure accounts for
serial dependence in forecast errors, while the use of blocks preserves the timeseries structure of the loss differentials. This is particularly important in volatility
forecasting settings, where forecast errors are typically autocorrelated and exhibit
clustering.

whereas the fusion model is not retained. Under MSE, CNND remains in the MCS

Explainable AI Results
This section examines how the proposed models form their predictions and which
intraday patterns they exploit. We consider two complementary levels: (i) intraday
attributions for the daily CNN and (ii) horizon-level contributions in the fusion
model. Together, these results provide a coherent view of how high-frequency
dynamics and multi-horizon information shape volatility forecasts.
5.1
Intraday Attributions (Daily CNN)
We employ gradient-based attribution, Grad-CAM (Selvaraju et al., 2017), to
identify which regions of the input images contribute most to model predictions.

Table 4 shows that effective contributions differ substantially from raw fusion

forecast. The discrepancy between fusion weights and contribution shares reflects
differences in the scale and variability of the underlying horizon-specific signals.
While the daily component receives the largest weight, its corresponding predictions
exhibit lower variability, resulting in a relatively small contribution in absolute
terms. In contrast, weekly and monthly components produce more variable signals,
leading to larger effective contributions despite smaller weights. This highlights
that parameter magnitudes alone might not be informative concerning model
importance in hybrid architectures, where both weights and input distributions
jointly determine the final prediction.
A clear regime dependence emerges. In low-volatility periods, longer horizons

lear regime dependence emerges. In low-volatility periods, longer horizons
dominate, with weekly and monthly components accounting for over 90% of the

This behavior is economically intuitive. During stable periods, volatility evolves
smoothly and is driven by persistent components, whereas in turbulent markets,
short-term shocks become more relevant. The fusion network therefore acts as an

depending on market conditions.

Conclusion
This study examines whether deep learning applied to intraday data can improve
forecasts of next-day realized volatility. We propose an image-based CNN framework that transforms intraday returns into two-dimensional representations and
processes them using horizon-specific networks capturing daily, weekly, and monthly
dynamics. A HAR-style fusion model combines these signals, preserving economic
interpretability while enabling flexible nonlinear feature extraction.
Using minute-by-minute data for 30 DJIA stocks over 2005–2023, we find consistent
improvements in out-of-sample forecasting accuracy relative to HAR and GARCHtype benchmarks. While the fusion model often achieves the lowest forecast errors,
Model Confidence Set results indicate that models based on daily input images

owest forecast errors,
Model Confidence Set results indicate that models based on daily input images
provide the most robust performance across assets. Explainable AI analyses further
show that the models emphasize negative intraday returns and dynamically shift
attention toward short-horizon signals during periods of elevated volatility.
Overall, the results demonstrate that combining high-frequency information with
structured multi-horizon modeling improves both predictive accuracy and interpretability, highlighting the potential of image-based deep learning approaches for
volatility forecasting.
Future research may extend this framework to multi-step forecasting, alternative
input representations, and the evaluation of economic gains in applications such as
risk management and trading.

Motivated by the Heterogeneous Market Hypothesis, the HAR model is an additive cascade model of different partial volatility components. These volatility
components are presumed to be generated by the heterogeneous actions of market
actors, originating from differences in their time horizons. The model differentiates

Concluding remarks
We empirically examine the co-movement among equity markets around the world.
Based on a time-varying spatial model, we estimate the global co-movement of 38 countries as well as for subsamples of American, Asian-Paciﬁc and European countries from
1995 to 2020. Our approach not only is able to capture the time-variation within the
co-movement, but also accounts for increasing variances during event or crisis periods.
Using conﬁdence intervals, we are able to detect contagion, measured by a signiﬁcant
increase in co-movement during an event. First, our results indicate that contagion on
a global level occurred only once within the last 25 years, namely during the ﬁrst wave
of the Covid-19 pandemic in the ﬁrst quarter of 2020. Second, our results highlight that
equity

wave
of the Covid-19 pandemic in the ﬁrst quarter of 2020. Second, our results highlight that
equity market co-movement increased during the last two decades, in particular among
European countries, while generally exhibiting a high level of ﬂuctuation. In contrast,
standard approaches such as correlation analysis neglect the time-varying behavior of
co-movement. For this reason our results provide a more general view of co-movement
beyond pairwise correlation and highlight the high level of global equity market integration. Last, and in support of the ﬁndings by Forbes and Rigobon (2002), market
dynamics often considered as contagion can be rather described as interdependence
when accounting for time-varying variances.

The detection of informational leadership is a core issue in financial market microstructure.
We use effective group transfer entropy (EGTE) as a measure for the predictability of a
stochastic process using lagged observations on multiple related processes within the same
system. We propose an appropriate bootstrap to derive confidence bounds and show by
means of a simulation study that standard linear approaches in economics and finance,
such as vector autoregressions

ation study that standard linear approaches in economics and finance,
such as vector autoregressions and Granger-causality tests, are not well suited to detect
information transfer. We empirically examine the markets for cryptocurrencies using
intraday data and reveal that the dependencies are mostly of nonlinear nature, highlighting
the applicability of EGTE in the context of this new financial product.

According to Hasbrouck [12, p. 1175], price discovery whereby new information is incorporated into security prices is ‘‘the
most important product[s] of a security market’’. The information leader can hope to attract the largest number of traders
which has a positive impact on all aspects of market liquidity. Hence, knowing which market is the leading market, is not
only of interest to the trading platforms, but also to investors and regulators. In situations where

only of interest to the trading platforms, but also to investors and regulators. In situations where many similar financial
products are traded, it might be of interest which of these is the informational leader. However, as the law of one price
cannot be claimed to hold if different assets are considered, cointegration cannot be established. Resorting to a linear VAR
framework, tests of Granger-causality are therefore the main tool. The latter still allow to establish informational leadership
in the sense that the leader should Granger-cause the other entities while the respective asset itself is not predictable.
In this article, we propose to use effective group transfer entropy (EGTE) to measure to which extent a random variable
is affected by a group of other random variables. We show

autoregressive models and propose a suitable time series block-bootstrap procedure for EGTE, which allows to conduct
inference. Although transfer entropy and Granger-causality are equivalent for Gaussian variables [19], our simulation study
shows that Granger-causality might lead to wrong conclusions, if the underlying processes are related in a nonlinear way.
Additionally, we show that effective group transfer entropy is not impacted by structural breaks, which are often an issue in
economic and financial time series, caused by regulatory changes or periods of economic distress.

2. GTE estimation and inference
2.1. Group transfer entropy
Financial or economic systems often involve more than two variables. While commonly feedback effects between
different time series might exists, it is often sufficient to determine the extent to which each time series is dependent on the
past states of the system to identify the informational leader. We therefore use a transfer entropy based measure to quantify
the dependencies of one time series on past values of a group of other time series.

Financial return data commonly exhibit leptokurtic distributions, where the tail observations are of main interest, as

5. Conclusion
We propose to use effective group transfer entropy (EGTE) to measure the dependence of a stochastic process on lagged
values of other stochastic processes within a multivariate system. In particular within the area of economics and finance,
standard approaches and tools are based on linear

rticular within the area of economics and finance,
standard approaches and tools are based on linear models such as vector autoregressive models and Granger-causality
tests. Our simulation study shows that these approaches might result in misleading conclusions due to their restriction to
linear relationships. EGTE offers an interesting alternative approach, as it is able to capture more general forms of statistical
dependencies.
In our empirical analysis we examine intraday data on four different cryptocurrencies (Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin,
and Monero) and find that information transfer between cryptocurrency markets is mostly a nonlinear process, which

A B S T R A C T
We analyze the transmission of volatility between the oil, stock, gold, and currency markets using transfer
entropy. Our approach, which we denote by group transfer entropy, measures the overall sensitivity of a
process to lagged realizations of a group of other processes. We supplement our measure by a suitable block
bootstrap approach which allows to conduct inference. Our empirical analysis uses daily data of OVX, VIX,
GVZ, and EVZ from 2008 to 2017. The results show that oil and stock market volatility are the most affected
by past volatility changes in the other markets, which highlights the importance for investors to hedge
against this predictable risk transmission. Furthermore, we show that

ortance for investors to hedge
against this predictable risk transmission. Furthermore, we show that group transfer entropy can unveil
nonlinear dynamics beyond the standard vector autoregressive methodology and provides a useful basis for
forecast averaging.

strategies, adding commodities, such as oil or gold, to their portfolios
to achieve optimal risk diversiﬁcation. During the global ﬁnancial crisis in 2007/2008, however, contagion led to increasing uncertainty
across a wide range of markets, revealing the importance of a better understanding of volatility transmission mechanisms (Creti et al.,

due to the geopolitical and global economic framework. Such shocks
might increase oil price volatility, which in turn could affect exchange

5. Conclusion
We measure the interdependence of ﬁnancial time series by
effective group transfer entropy. This procedure circumvents the
issues involved in using partial transfer entropy (potential bias and
the requirement of very large datasets) and provides the possibility
to

entropy (potential bias and
the requirement of very large datasets) and provides the possibility
to detect non-linear dependencies, enlarging the realm of multivariate time series analysis.
In our empirical application we consider volatility indices of oil
(OVX), the US stock market (VIX), gold (GVZ), and the Euro/US Dollar
exchange rate (EVZ) in a post-crisis period. We ﬁnd signiﬁcant predictability of each variable, when using the group of the remaining
variables. We illustrate that a VAR analysis cannot fully capture the
dependence structure, and show that indeed the relationships are to
the largest extent non-linear. Consequently, empirical analyses relying on linear time series models underestimate the spillover effects.
Our results suggest that the oil and the stock market

es models underestimate the spillover effects.
Our results suggest that the oil and the stock market volatilities are
the most affected by volatility transmission from the other markets.
Finally, we show that our GTE estimates can be used to improve
volatility forecasts compared to a naïve forecast.

Abstract: We implement the VIX methodology on intraday data of a large set of individual equity
options. We thereby consider approaches based on monthly option contracts, weekly option contracts,
and a cubic spline interpolation approach. Relying on 1 min, 10 min, and 60 min model-free implied
volatility measures, we empirically examine the individual equity return–volatility relationship on
the intraday

easures, we empirically examine the individual equity return–volatility relationship on
the intraday level using quantile regressions. The results confirm a negative contemporaneous link
between stock returns and volatility, which is more pronounced in the tails of the distributions.
Our findings hint at behavioral biases causing the asymmetric return–volatility link rather than the
leverage and volatility-feedback effects.
Keywords: model-free implied volatility; individual equity options; intraday volatility; leverage;
quantile regressions

Volatility is a key input variable for assessing risk, pricing derivative products, and

introduces errors if strikes are too widely dispersed. As Jiang and Tian (2005) showed,

reliable MFIV estimates can be obtained if the truncation point of each tail is 3.5 standard
deviations (SDs)3 from the at-the-money forward price F0. They further show that the

negligible below strike-price increments of 0.35 SDs.

4. Analyzing the Intraday Return–Volatility Relationship
The 1 min frequency of the MFIV measures allows us to examine whether specific
relationships and stylized facts also hold on an intraday and individual equity level. So
far, the return–volatility relationship in financial markets has been analyzed extensively.
While theoretically higher risks have to be compensated by higher returns, indicating
a positive relationship, empirical studies mostly document a negative and potentially
asymmetric relationship between returns and changes in volatility6. Concerning equity
markets, fundamental

tric relationship between returns and changes in volatility6. Concerning equity
markets, fundamental theories have been put forward to explain this negative link. The
leverage hypothesis suggested by Black (1976) and Christie (1982) explains an increase
in equity volatility with a decline in the value of the firm, while the volatility-feedback
hypothesis associates an increase in volatility with higher expected returns and lower
current prices7. As explained by Bollerslev et al. (2006), both theories differ mainly by their
implied direction of causality.
More recently, Hibbert et al. (2008) (among others) proposed a behavioral perspective
and associated the negative return–volatility relationship with the presence of different
groups of investors. These groups may differ with respect to

tionship with the presence of different
groups of investors. These groups may differ with respect to the extent to which they are
prone to behavioral biases, such as representativeness, affect, and extrapolation biases. In
contrast to the leverage and volatility-feedback hypothesis, which may take time to establish
and, therefore, are more plausible at lower frequencies, behavioral biases may very well be
present even at intraday frequencies. However, existing studies on the return–volatility
relationship at higher frequencies are rare and have focused mostly on equity indices8.
Therefore, we use our intraday MFIV measures to examine the intraday return–volatility
relationship for the individual equities in our sample.

5. Conclusions
We implement the CBOE VIX method on intraday option data for individual equities. In doing so, we analyze the data quality with respect to the MFIV calculation. Our
descriptive data analysis reveals that, for 138 individual equities, weekly options exhibit
a sufficient range of strike prices to avoid significant truncation errors according to Jiang
and Tian (2005). Descriptive analyses of MFIV sample averages based on weekly options,
monthly options, and a cubic

. Descriptive analyses of MFIV sample averages based on weekly options,
monthly options, and a cubic spline interpolation approach reveal only marginal differences. We find the intraday individual equity MFIV measures to exhibit a similar diurnal
pattern as implied volatility indices, such as the VIX, with higher levels after opening hours
and declining levels until closing hours.
We use our estimates to analyze the intraday return volatility–relationship using 1, 10,
and 60 min data. We find a negative relationship between returns and volatility changes,
which is significant for most of our sample stocks when considering contemporaneous
returns. The stronger the link, the lower the frequency. For lagged returns, the effect is less
evident. Quantile regressions reveal a clear inverted

quency. For lagged returns, the effect is less
evident. Quantile regressions reveal a clear inverted U-shaped pattern when considering
contemporaneous returns, which again becomes less evident for lagged returns. These
findings indicate that behavioral biases rather than the fundamental theories of leverage
or volatility-feedback effects cause the asymmetric link between returns and volatility.
Despite offering a starting point for calculating and analyzing individual equity MFIV at
high frequencies, our approach comes with some limitations. The standard VIX calculation
method is prone to have a specific cut-off rule to determine what option quotes are used
in computing the VIX. As outlined by Andersen et al. (2015), this may bias the calculated
MFIV measures. Andersen et al. (2015)

tlined by Andersen et al. (2015), this may bias the calculated
MFIV measures. Andersen et al. (2015) offered an improved approach, termed the Corridor
Implied Volatility, which alleviates the potential bias of the standard measure. Moreover,
Andersen et al. (2015) noted that the relationship between returns and volatility is prone
to jumps and co-jumps in both series and may be more complex depending on different
regimes. Subsequently, while our empirical analysis of the return–volatility relationship
may offer a valid starting point, future research should be conducted accounting for a
potential dynamic nature of this relationship. Overall, our individual equity MFIV measure
opens up avenues for further research. The forward-looking nature of implied volatility
may have merits for

p avenues for further research. The forward-looking nature of implied volatility
may have merits for volatility prediction on an intraday level, as well as on a daily level
for individual equities. Moreover, the derived time series of intraday MFIV measures
will allow us to assess the imminent effect of news on volatility relying on time series
models. They also offer the opportunity to address the impact of attention and sentiment
measures at such high frequencies. It will also be of great interest to extend the sampling
period throughout the pandemic period and analyze the impact of lockdown situations
on the stock volatilities of different industries. In general, MFIV measures also allow
a decomposition into the conditional variance of stock returns and the equity variance
premium,

llow
a decomposition into the conditional variance of stock returns and the equity variance
premium, where the latter has been shown to possess predictive power for stock returns.
The proposed MFIV measures can also be used to decompose volatility into a systematic
risk component and idiosyncratic risk, using the VIX index as a measure of market risk.
Such idiosyncratic risk measures, then again, may yield interesting insights into investors’
risk perceptions and resulting investment decisions, potentially depending on and varying
during high and low market volatility regimes.

1. Introduction
The last decade has seen increasing globalization and improved
technology concerning the trading of ﬁnancial assets. This development has sharpened competition among stock exchanges around
the world, in particular where exchanges compete for the same
crowd of investors, as in the

s around
the world, in particular where exchanges compete for the same
crowd of investors, as in the case of cross-listed stocks. In order
to attract investors, exchanges have to provide an efﬁcient trading
environment, where information is incorporated into prices as
quickly as possible. This renders the contributions of each trading
venue to the price discovery process of the common stock a quality
feature.
This paper contributes to the current literature by proposing an
alternative price discovery measure (information share). Our information share is based on Russell’s (1999) autoregressive conditional intensity model (ACI). This bivariate intensity approach
accounts for the informational content of time between consecutive quoted price changes within a market as well as the timing

ional content of time between consecutive quoted price changes within a market as well as the timing
interdependencies between the price processes on both markets.
In contrast to the commonly applied Hasbrouck (1995) methodology, we exploit the irregular occurrence of price changes and deliver a unique information share. We apply our new measure to
Canadian stocks that are traded on the Toronto Stock Exchange
(TSX) and cross-listed on the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE).
Furthermore, we examine potential determinants of information
shares in a cross-sectional analysis.
Evidence from previous studies suggests that price discovery for
cross-listed stocks mainly takes place in the home market. Eun and
Sabherwal (2003) examine a sample of US-listed Canadian stocks

The main drawback of the Hasbrouck (1995) approach is that it
merely delivers upper and lower bounds for an information share.
The method requires equidistant sampled quotes and, depending
on the chosen sampling frequency, the information share bounds
can diverge considerably. Consequently, the conclusions concerning the leading market are rather vague (see Hupperets and Menkveld (2002) and Korczak and Phylaktis (2010)).1 We take an
alternative view on how to quantify the informational linkage between different exchanges trading the same underlying asset which
is motivated by the following considerations. First, as acknowledged
in the ﬁnancial markets literature (e.g. Dufour and Engle, 2000;
Engle, 2000; Engle and Lunde, 2003; Frijns and Schotman, 2009),
the irregular occurrence of trades

;
Engle, 2000; Engle and Lunde, 2003; Frijns and Schotman, 2009),
the irregular occurrence of trades and quotes and the time between
consecutive ﬁnancial market events reveal the dynamics of price responses to new information in the market. Hence, arbitrary sampling
schemes used to obtain regularly spaced data neglect this aspect of
the price dynamics and induce an undesirable loss of information.
Second, as pointed out by Hasbrouck (1995), ‘‘... the information
share measures who moves ﬁrst in the process of price adjustment.’’
If price discovery is indeed understood as which market ‘‘moves
ﬁrst’’, an information share measure that is derived from a model
that directly accounts for the irregular sequence and timing of the
price process seems to be a straightforward approach. We exploit

rregular sequence and timing of the
price process seems to be a straightforward approach. We exploit
the irregularity of high frequency stock market data and propose
an alternative information share by modeling the arrival rates
(intensities) of the price processes using Russell’s (1999) ACI model.
Within this framework the dynamics of the intensity functions are
driven by innovations that allow for a ﬂexible interaction and simultaneously affect the conditional intensities in both markets.
In the case of cross-listed securities the law of one price applies
and deviations from the equilibrium price can only be transitory.
Consequently, when prices in both markets deviate, adjustment
has to take place to restore the equilibrium. The main question is
which market moves ﬁrst and which

has to take place to restore the equilibrium. The main question is
which market moves ﬁrst and which markets adjust to restore
the equilibrium price? If the market event that caused the deviation was due to new information, the arbitrage relation between
prices in parallel markets forces an immediate incorporation of
new information into the other market’s price thereby increasing
its intensity. This translates into positive spillover effects due to
the innovations. We argue that the larger the effect of an innovation in one market on the other market’s intensity, the greater is
its intensity-based information share, i.e. the information ﬂow that
originates from this trading venue.
We empirically analyze the price discovery process of Canadian
stocks traded on the TSX and cross-listed on

rically analyze the price discovery process of Canadian
stocks traded on the TSX and cross-listed on the NYSE. Our results
show the TSX to be a clear leader in the price discovery process.
With an average information share of 73%, the contribution of
the TSX is more pronounced than indicated by Eun and Sabherwal
(2003).
We also examine potential determinants of a market’s contribution to price discovery by conducting a cross-sectional regression
of the intensity-based information share on stock-speciﬁc factors
and liquidity-related variables.
Eun and Sabherwal (2003), Korczak and Phylaktis (2010), Grammig et al. (2005) and Frijns et al. (2010) among others analyze the
determinants of price discovery in the home and foreign market
and ﬁnd a positive relation between the contributions to

and ﬁnd a positive relation between the contributions to price discovery and liquidity. In line with this research, our results show
that liquidity proxies are the only variables that are related to a
market’s price determination. This implies that providing an efﬁcient and liquid trading environment is of particular interest for
small national stock exchanges that seek to maintain their dominance in the price discovery process of cross-listed stocks.

Prior to estimation, the data have to be thinned in order to reduce the amount of noise and retrieve a time series of price-relevant events. Following Engle and Russell (1997), Bowsher (2007)
and Bauwens and Hautsch (2006), the quote data are thinned using
a function of price marks. Bid and ask midquotes are calculated and
absolute cumulative price changes constructed that are retained
whenever they exceeded a speciﬁc threshold. Generally, ﬁnance
literature does not provide explicit guidance concerning the thinning of data for point process modeling. Engle and Russell (1997)
ﬁrst introduced a thinning rule to the literature and choose a rather
small value of 0.0005 US$ which in their sample corresponds to
half the largest observed spread. Bauwens and Hautsch (2006) selected threshold

ample corresponds to

analysis the mean spread on the TSX is 0.08 CAD and on the NYSE
0.06 US$. We set threshold values to 0.025 Canadian Dollars for the
TSX, which, after accounting for the exchange rate and the minimum tick size, corresponds to 0.02 US Dollars for the NYSE price
changes. Our threshold corresponds roughly to one third of the
mean spread and half of the median spread on the two markets

2.3. Intensity-based information shares
In order to measure contributions to price discovery, we draw
our attention to the cross effects of the conditional intensities associated with quote changes on the home and foreign markets. As
prices in both markets refer to the same underlying asset, the
law of one price holds. This implies that informative price events
occurring in one market will subsequently be incorporated into
the price of the other market to offset arbitrage

one market will subsequently be incorporated into
the price of the other market to offset arbitrage opportunities. Consequently, unexpected quote adjustments in one market trigger
price events in the other market and increase the other market’s
conditional intensity. Analogously, the unexpected absence of
price changes in one market reduces the other market’s intensity.
These interactions entail positive cross effects. We propose using
the size of the markets’ cross effects to measure the relative importance of a market in the price discovery process.
We start by examining the long-run impacts of an innovation
on the conditional intensities by analyzing the full dynamics of
the markets’ interdependencies.

5. Conclusion
The decisions made by investors and companies, respectively,
regarding whether to invest or list their stocks depends on an exchange’s ability to provide a prospering trading environment. As a
result of increasing globalization and improved technology, small
national exchanges are beginning to fear that they will lose their
attractiveness for investors and companies. In particular, within
the context of international cross-listed stocks, it is of paramount
concern for a national stock exchange to remain the dominant
market with regard to price discovery.
We propose a new approach to measuring the contribution of
trading venues to the price discovery process of internationally
cross-listed stocks. We use a bivariate intensity approach as an
alternative to the commonly applied

cross-listed stocks. We use a bivariate intensity approach as an
alternative to the commonly applied vector error correction model,
in order to take into account the irregularity of the data. Based on
the autoregressive conditional intensity model developed by Russell (1999), contributions to price discovery are measured by modeling the interdependencies of the trading processes in both
markets. In contrast to the Hasbrouck (1995) approach, the intensity-based information shares deliver unique results rather than
upper and lower bounds. Furthermore, we show that the suggested
approach provides a more accurate means to determine the dominant market in the price discovery process.
In our empirical application of this measure to the Canadian
context we examine stocks which are listed on the

irical application of this measure to the Canadian
context we examine stocks which are listed on the TSX as well as
on the NYSE. We ﬁnd that trading on the TSX plays the most
important role. This conﬁrms previous results by Korczak and
Phylaktis (2010), Eun and Sabherwal (2003), and Grammig et al.
(2005), who also analyze Canadian stocks. We show that the leadership of the TSX is even more pronounced than indicated by previous studies. The average TSX information share amounts to 73%.
In order to explore potential determinants of a market’s information share, we conduct cross-sectional regressions and like
Grammig et al. (2005), Eun and Sabherwal (2003), and Korczak
and Phylaktis (2010) ﬁnd that liquidity contributes positively to
a market’s price determination.
Generally, our

s (2010) ﬁnd that liquidity contributes positively to
a market’s price determination.
Generally, our intensity-based unique information share presents an appealing alternative to the Hasbrouck (1995) information shares when analyzing price discovery using high frequency
data, as it accounts for the irregular spacing of the data.

A B S T R A C T
We demonstrate the possibility of predicting the millionaire status of an externally-owned Ethereum
account based on information queried out of the Blockchain and features describing its role in the
network based on node embedding techniques. These features are fed into artificial neural nets and
used for status prediction within a systematic model selection process. We report key methodological
insights about training and comparing cross-validated deep and shallow neural networks that yield
up to 82 percent testset accuracy in predicting the millionaire status of account users.

This paper outlines an approach for extracting and structuring Ethereum transactions using theory-informed features
about structural roles, homophily, a subject’s transaction
behavior, and its financial network and conduct a systematic
model selection procedure based on artificial neural nets
against a customer-lifetime-value background. We predict
the millionaire status of an externally-owned Ethereum account based on information derived from the Blockchain
as well as features describing their role in the network
which are derived by applying node embedding techniques.

Loss function:
For binary classification tasks, binary Cross-Entropy is
reported as the standard loss function, calculating the average insecurity of the model when making a classification.
While we are aware that the choice of loss and activation
functions might be crucial in some applications, as outlined
for instance by Soares & Pereira (2016), we decided to
stick with standard choices to focus on the overall model
architecture in the selection process (deep versus shallow).
Furthermore, previous applications, in particular within
finance and economics, such as the one by Orimoloye et al.
(2020), choose cross-entropy as a loss function as well and
also conclude that paired with the ReLU activation function

Activation function and gradient stabilizers:
Considering that we train deep neural nets as well, and
having to deal with potential vanishing or exploding gradient
problem ReLU was chosen as an activation function considering its stability against this issue (Tan & Lim, 2019).
As there is no disadvantage of using ReLU in shallow
networks, it is chosen as the hidden layer activation function
throughout all our network architectures. In addition, for
models with more than two layers, two more countermeasures against vanishing gradients have been applied. First,
batch normalization was included in all hidden layers to

nishing gradients have been applied. First,
batch normalization was included in all hidden layers to keep
the gradients stable during backpropagation (Bjorck et al.,
2018). Second, the ReLU-compliant He initialization was
used, preventing the model from using too small or too large
weights at the initialization, which could otherwise result in
vanishing or exploding gradients right with the first epoch
(S. K. Kumar, 2017).
Regularization
To stabilize a neural net against overfitting, several regularization measures such as dropout rates or penalty terms
might be helpful. Depending on the penalty term lambda, the
weight of a node will converge against zero if its contribution
to a smaller loss is lower than the increase in complexity it
causes. Contrary to the alternative L2 norm, the L1

loss is lower than the increase in complexity it
causes. Contrary to the alternative L2 norm, the L1 norm
can eventually forced weights down to zero (Friedman,
2017). Although the risk exists that the shrunken weights,
in general, intensify the vanishing gradient problem, it is
more apparent for the L2 norm, as the values do not reach
0. This property makes L1 more attractive for deep learning
approaches. This shrinkage of uninformative parameters
down to zero should reduce the complexity of the model,
making it less prone to overfitting (Gulli & Pal, 2017).
Due to our high number of features, dropout rates 𝑑∈
[0, 0.1], and L1 penalty terms 𝜆∈[0, 0.05] are applied when

Optimizer:
When choosing a flexible and deep network, successful
convergence can be difficult to reach, as the increased depth
leads to increased resistance to the training process in terms
of letting the gradients smoothly flow through the network.
Strongly connected to the success of convergence is the
choice of the optimizing algorithm. Although Stochastic
Gradient Descent is the standard, modern models often
rely on recently developed alternatives such as the Adam
optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014). Contrary to Stochastic
Gradient Descent, where the

optimizer (Kingma & Ba, 2014). Contrary to Stochastic
Gradient Descent, where the learning rate stays fixed, the
adaptions calculated by the Adam optimizer depend on the
estimated first moment and the estimated second moment of
the gradient.
Thus, instead of having updates that depend on the current
gradient, the updates depend on a general "trend", making it
less sensitive to local minima and more reliable if confronted
with noisy gradients (Gulli et al., 2019). Empirical results
demonstrate that the Adam optimizer works well in practice
and compares favorably to other stochastic optimization
methods (Kingma & Ba, 2014, p. 1). Given these properties,
all models in the presented work are trained with Adam as
an optimizer using the default hyperparameter values.

We examine the price discovery contributions of cryptocurrency exchanges in the presence
of market microstructure noise. Cryptocurrency markets exhibit a decisively higher level of
microstructure noise compared with the NYSE or NASDAQ. Therefore, traditional measures
of price discovery could be biased. To overcome this concern, we draw on the information
leadership share proposed by Putnin, š (2013); by leveraging this information, we ﬁnd that
Bitﬁnex is the leader in the price discovery process. These results highlight the importance of
accounting for different levels of noise when evaluating price discovery contributions.

1. Introduction
Cryptocurrencies are traded on more than 300 exchanges worldwide, and across these exchanges, the price discrepancies
reach up to 1000 USD for the same cryptocurrency. Deﬁning their fundamental value thus is diﬃcult, because it is unclear
which exchange to consider. In a setting in which multiple exchanges trade the same asset, the most informative price exists
in the market where price discovery is highest, such that its prices reﬂect new information faster than prices reported on other
markets. In a cryptocurrency context, the situation is more complex, due to considerably greater uncertainty about its fundamental value. That is, cryptocurrencies likely reﬂect the value of some expected future beneﬁt, but the high

alue. That is, cryptocurrencies likely reﬂect the value of some expected future beneﬁt, but the high volatility inherent
in these markets suggests a diﬃcult valuation process. At the extreme, we might even ask if prices on these markets reﬂect any
information at all, or whether they are nothing but noise.
Different levels of microstructure noise distort the traditional price discovery measures of Gonzalo and Granger (1995) and
Hasbrouck (1995) in such a way that the measures ultimately indicate noise avoidance rather than a market’s true contribution
to the fundamental value. Considering these concerns, we provide a detailed description of the noise inherent in our sample

(1995) and Hasbrouck (1995), researchers have had two measures at their disposal, both of which can numerically quantify
contributions to price discovery. Accordingly, these measures are used frequently, especially for stock markets (Booth et al.,
1999; So and Tse, 2004; Grammig et al., 2005; Comerton-Forde and Putnin, š, 2015), though also for commodities like gold
(Hauptﬂeisch et al., 2016) or agricultural products (Dimpﬂet al., 2017). However, some issues remain; for example, Hasbrouck
(1995) information share is not unique, and both measures potentially are prone to market microstructure frictions. The ﬁrst
issue has been resolved by

issue has been resolved by Lien and Shrestha (2012) and Grammig and Peter (2013). The second issue, which is more relevant
for our research, has been addressed by Yan and Zivot (2010) and Putnin, š (2013), who suggest combining Gonzalo and Granger
(1995) ad Hasbrouck (1995) measures to obtain an information share that is robust to the potential bias induced by different
levels of microstructure noise.

3. Market details and data description
Our sample consists of ﬁve cryptocurrencies traded simultaneously on three exchanges. We use intraday transaction data of
Bitcoin (BTC), Ethereum Classic (ETC), Ethereum (ETH), Litecoin (LTC), and Monero (XMR), traded against the U.S. dollar (USD).
The data sets consist of all transactions on three cryptocurrency exchanges, Bitﬁnex, Kraken, and Poloniex, which are among the
most liquid exchanges during the time period considered (March 2017 to November 2017). These three exchanges also account
for roughly 30% of Bitcoin trading volume during the sample period, among more than 300 exchanges.2 The chosen coins rank
among the top 10 with respect to traded volume, led by Bitcoin,

00 exchanges.2 The chosen coins rank
among the top 10 with respect to traded volume, led by Bitcoin, which attracted up to 80% of the total cryptocurrency market
capitalization at the beginning of our sample period.3
The three trading venues differ on several features, as detailed in Table 1. The minimum tick size, for example, differs substantially among exchanges and is not stable over time. For Bitcoin, the range is from 0.0001 on Poloniex to 0.1 on Kraken at
the end of our sample period. Tick size on Bitﬁnex was 0.005 until October 24, 2017, when the exchange introduced a ﬂexible
minimum tick size to ensure that one tick equals a range of 10–25 USD.4

6. Conclusion
We examine the microstructure noise component and its impact on price discovery among three trading platforms for ﬁve
cryptocurrencies. The levels of microstructure noise differ substantially across exchanges. Although the tick size, bid-ask spread,
and the number of transactions may have some role in explaining these differences, their impact on the noise component is not
clear-cut. A special case is Poloniex, which only offers trading against a stable coin rather than against ﬁat currencies, so it likely
creates an additional source of noise. Our results show that cryptocurrency traders face the highest noise level on Poloniex.
Overall, prices on any of the cryptocurrency exchanges are not as informative as

level on Poloniex.
Overall, prices on any of the cryptocurrency exchanges are not as informative as those on the NYSE or NASDAQ, resulting in
SNRs that are about half the magnitude as those resulting from the NYSE or NASDAQ. That is, cryptocurrency prices reﬂect more
than just noise, but they have not yet reach the level of informativeness of stock prices.
Our price discovery analysis reveals that overall, Bitﬁnex is the leading cryptocurrency exchange, followed by Poloniex and
Kraken. Yan and Zivot (2010) and Putnin, š (2013) argue that different levels of microstructure noise prevent traditional information share measures, such as those proposed by Gonzalo and Granger (1995) and Hasbrouck (1995), from offering correct
identiﬁcation of contributions to price discovery. We show that for

identiﬁcation of contributions to price discovery. We show that for Poloniex – the market with the highest noise level – traditional measures suggest a lower information share compared to the information leadership share proposed by Putnin, š (2013),
which accounts for the noise component in the price series. In other words, the higher level of microstructure noise on Poloniex
overshadows its contribution to price discovery, such that traditional measures cannot reliably detect the true contribution.

Applying the Cholesky decomposition involves ruling out certain contemporaneous effects. The ordering 
of the markets becomes important as shocks in the market ordered first can instantly influence all other 
markets, while the contemporaneous effects of the market ordered last are restricted to zero. This results in

5 Conclusion
We propose a Markov switching framework to model price discovery between the CDS and the corporate bond 
market. The major advantage of our approach lies in delivering a unique measure for the markets’ contribution 
to the price discovery process as opposed to the Hasbrouck (1995) measure, which yields a range. At the same

rice discovery process as opposed to the Hasbrouck (1995) measure, which yields a range. At the same 
time, the Markov property allows for a regime-switching behavior of information shocks in the two markets.
Analyzing a sample of 22 iTraxx companies, we determine the CDS market as the informationally dominant market. The CDS market information share even increases in periods marked by high volatility. We also 
examine potential determinants for the information share measures. The results support previously reported 
evidence of a positive link between liquidity and information shares. Firm-specific characteristics such as 
market capitalization, leverage, or affiliation to a specific industry are not found to be statistically significant.

This paper shows how to quantify and test for the information flow between two time series with
Shannon transfer entropy and Rényi transfer entropy using the R package RTransferEntropy. We discuss
the methodology, the bias correction applied to calculate effective transfer entropy and outline how
to conduct statistical inference. Furthermore, we describe the package in detail and demonstrate its
functionality by means of several simulated processes and present an application to financial time
series.

Our package RTransferEntropy [12] offers a user-friendly tool

2. Estimating directional dependencies using transfer entropy
2.1. Transfer entropy and Rényi transfer entropy
Transfer entropy is rooted in information theory and based
on the concept of Shannon entropy as a measure of uncertainty.
In 1928, Hartley [13] introduced a measure for information calculated as the logarithm of the number of all possible symbol

The transfer entropy estimates are biased in small samples

drawing values from the observed time series J and realigning

between J and I. As a result, TJshuffled→I(k, l)

The R package RTransferEntropy offers straightforward routines
to quantify and test the information flow between two time
series measurements with Shannon and Rényi transfer entropy.
The main function is transfer_entropy(), which returns the

7. Conclusions
We present and outline empirical as well as theoretical aspects
concerning the R package RTransferEntropy, which provides a convenient tool to estimate Shannon and Rényi transfer entropy, both
well-established measures derived from information theory. In
particular, the package calculates effective transfer entropy using
a simple finite sample bias correction and provides the means
to conduct statistical inference, which is an important aspect in
every application across research areas.
Since transfer entropy is

, which is an important aspect in
every application across research areas.
Since transfer entropy is a nonparametric measure and detects
any statistical dependence between time series, it is applied
in various disciplines such as economics, biometrics, or neuroscience. We demonstrate the functionality of the package by
means of multiple examples based on simulated processes as well
as an empirical application to financial time series. The latter
illustrates how transfer entropy can be used to detect interdependencies between individual stocks and the market as a whole
and how Rényi transfer entropy allows to give more weight to
tail events in their contribution to the overall information flow.

Price discovery in the markets for credit risk: 
a Markov switching approach
DOI 10.1515/snde-2015-0032
Abstract: We examine price discovery in the Credit Default Swap and corporate bond market. Using a Markov 
switching framework enables us to analyze the dynamic behavior of the information shares during tranquil 
and crisis periods. The results show that price discovery takes place mostly on the CDS market. The importance of the CDS market even increases during the more volatile crisis periods. According to a cross sectional 
analysis liquidity is the main determinant of a market’s contribution to price discovery. During the crisis 
period, however, we also find a positive link between leverage and CDS

discovery. During the crisis 
period, however, we also find a positive link between leverage and CDS market information shares. Overall 
the results indicate that price discovery measures and their determinants change during tranquil and crisis 
periods, which emphasizes the importance of more flexible frameworks, such as Markov switching models.
Keywords: corporate bond; credit default swap; Markov switching; price discovery; unique information share.
JEL classification: C14; G15.
1 Introduction
The markets for credit risk have recently attracted great attention in finance literature. Particularly, the reaction of the credit default swap (CDS) market to the crisis period of 2007–2009 has been analyzed, as it allows 
researchers to derive information that may help to maintain financial

In this context, information transmission between markets is of paramount interest. One of the key questions 
is how the price discovery process reacts to changes in the market environment, such as a serious financial 
crisis. In order to examine this issue, we use a Markov switching framework to analyze the dynamics of the 
price discovery process between the markets for credit risk, i.e. the CDS and corporate bond markets, during 
tranquil and crisis periods. Furthermore, we examine potential factors that influence a market’s importance 
for the price discovery process and whether these change during more volatile times.

Applying the Cholesky decomposition involves ruling out certain contemporaneous effects. The ordering 
of the markets becomes important as shocks in the market ordered first can instantly influence all other 
markets, while the contemporaneous effects of the market ordered last are restricted to zero. This results in 
an upper bound estimate for the information share of the market ordered first and a lower bound estimate of 
the market ordered last. Permuting the ordering yields lower and upper bounds for each market.

5 Conclusion
We propose a Markov switching framework to model price discovery between the CDS and the corporate bond 
market. The major advantage of our approach lies in delivering a unique measure for the markets’ contribution 
to the price discovery process as opposed to the Hasbrouck (1995) measure, which yields a range. At the same

rice discovery process as opposed to the Hasbrouck (1995) measure, which yields a range. At the same 
time, the Markov property allows for a regime-switching behavior of information shocks in the two markets.
Analyzing a sample of 22 iTraxx companies, we determine the CDS market as the informationally dominant market. The CDS market information share even increases in periods marked by high volatility. We also 
examine potential determinants for the information share measures. The results support previously reported 
evidence of a positive link between liquidity and information shares. Firm-specific characteristics such as 
market capitalization, leverage, or affiliation to a specific industry are not found to be statistically significant.

the discovery of the informationally efﬁcient price. We exploit salient distributional features of multivariate ﬁnancial price processes to uniquely determine these contributions,
thereby resolving the main drawback of the widely used Hasbrouck (1995) methodology, which merely provides upper and lower bounds of a market’s information share. We

Information shares are deﬁned as each market’s contribution to the variance
of the efﬁcient price innovations. However, this variance cannot be decomposed
without further restrictions when the observable market price innovations are
contemporaneously correlated. The correlation increases with longer sampling

matrix decomposition implies an informational hierarchy of markets that is hardly

B.
Tail Dependence in a Microstructural Model
The identiﬁcation of idiosyncratic innovations (the key to unique information
shares) is a prevalent problem in various ﬁelds of economics. For that purpose,
macroeconomic studies exploit theory-based restrictions on short- and/or longrun impacts of idiosyncratic shocks. However, ﬁnance theory does not suggest
any constraints on the long-run effects of idiosyncratic price innovations (i.e., on
ξ′B), nor any direct constraints on B. Hence, the indeterminacy of Hasbrouck’s
(1995) information share measure remained a caveat for 15 years.1

Markets for credit risk are particularly interesting for the application of our
methodology because movements in liquidity premia arguably explain a large proportion of the total variation in credit spreads (see also Collin-Dufresne, Goldstein,
and Spencer (2001)). The microstructural reference model presented in Section

price changes, which can be exploited to compute unique information shares.

Conclusion
“Where does price discovery take place?” is a key question in empirical ﬁnance. It is frequently raised in the context of studies on the competition for order
ﬂow between traditional and alternative trading platforms, national and international exchanges, and parallel markets for traditional and innovative ﬁnancial instruments.
Hasbrouck’s (1995) methodology is the standard approach to addressing this
research question empirically. He proposes to estimate the information share for
each of the parallel markets on which ﬁnancial instruments linked by the law of
one price are traded. Information shares result from decomposing the variance of

inked by the law of
one price are traded. Information shares result from decomposing the variance of
the innovations to the market prices’ common stochastic trend, the efﬁcient price
of the security.
The competitive edge of Hasbrouck’s (1995) information shares over alternative methodologies used to measure contributions to price discovery is widely
accepted (see also Lehmann (2002)). However, most applications suffer from a
lack of identiﬁcation, since the contemporaneous dependence structure of market price innovations cannot be disentangled without further restrictions. As a

Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis
solution, Hasbrouck (1995) suggests a Cholesky decomposition of the covariance
matrix of the market price innovations, thereby assuming a hierarchical ordering of markets that is hardly ever justiﬁable. In empirical work, researchers often
resort to permuting the ordering of the markets, which yields upper and lower
bounds of information shares rather than a unique measure. These bounds can be
so wide that it is impossible to determine even the leading market.
The present paper resolves the problem of indeterminate information shares
by exploiting the informational content of distributional properties of ﬁnancial
prices. We show that different correlations of contemporaneous price innovations
in the tails and in the center of the

at different correlations of contemporaneous price innovations
in the tails and in the center of the distributions deliver the information necessary to determine unique information shares. Tail dependence of this kind can be
caused by the design of the trading process, which may induce market-speciﬁc
liquidity effects. Since in most applications of the Hasbrouck (1995) methodology the market structures are clearly different—which is why alternative trading
platforms emerge in the ﬁrst place—our methodology presents an appealing solution. With regard to the pricing of credit risk, it is the higher liquidity of the CDS
market compared to the corporate bond market that sharpens the ﬁnding that informational leadership lay with the credit derivatives market during the precrisis
period.

We have applied the new methodology to data sampled on a low (daily) frequency at which the contemporaneous correlation of market price innovations, the
source of the indeterminacy of Hasbrouck’s (1995) information share measure,
is strong. Indeed, many interesting securities trade on OTC dealer markets that
may generate a public quote only once a day. If shortening the sampling interval
is possible, the indeterminacy problem will usually be mitigated, because then the
contemporaneous correlation tends to be smaller. However, the advantages of
ultra-high-frequency data have to be balanced against their drawbacks: Veritable microstructure noise, like inaccurate timing of quotes, may bias the

inst their drawbacks: Veritable microstructure noise, like inaccurate timing of quotes, may bias the results.
Overall, the methodology presented in this paper seems to be best suited for
low- to medium-frequency data where going to a ﬁne interval of observation is
either impossible or not advisable. When quality ultra-high-frequency data are
available, intensity-based models, which account for the irregular spacing of the
data in time (see also Hautsch (2004)), could be employed to ﬁlter price-relevant
events on parallel markets and to construct alternative measures of price discovery. Kehrle and Peter (2013) take a 1st step in that direction, but a coherent link
to the efﬁcient price process, comparable to Hasbrouck’s (1995) framework, has

We present empirical evidence that collective investor behavior can be inferred from large-scale Wikipedia

Drawing upon Shannon transfer entropy, a model-free measure that 
considers any kind of statistical dependence between two time series, we quantify the statistical information flow 
between daily company-specific Wikipedia searches and stock returns for a sample of 447 stocks from 2008 to 
2017. The resulting stock-wise measures on information transmission are then used as a signal within a hy­
pothetical trading strategy. The results evidence the predictive power of Wikipedia searches and are in line with 
the previously documented notion of buying pressure revealed by online investor attention and the trading 
patterns of retail investors.

roscience, or statistical physics and increasingly attracts attention of 
financial market researchers.1

3. Data 
To test for and quantify the information transfer between Wikipedia 
searches and individual-level stock returns, we combine data from two 
different sources. On the one hand, stock prices for a broad range of 
listed companies. On the other hand, daily count data on Wikipedia 
searches for each corresponding company's Wikipedia page – or, to be 
more precise, the number of views per Wikipedia page. Stock in­
formation is sourced from the Thomson One database and contains

5. A simple application to stock trading 
We design a hypothetical trading strategy for Wikipedia stocks that 
uses retail investor attention as measured by a changes in page views as 
a trading signal. This approach is in line with Preis et al. (2013) and

a trading signal. This approach is in line with Preis et al. (2013) and 
Moat et al. (2013), who utilize investment strategies to infer collective 
investor behavior from online search data. See also the portfolio sorting

et al. (2011). Thus, the goal is not to design a realistic and profitable 
trading strategy but to use a simple framework to test whether the in­
formation transmission from Wikipedia page views to stock returns 
implied by significant transfer entropy estimates documented in the 
previous section can be translated into buying and selling signals.

6. Conclusion 
In this paper, we present empirical evidence that for a significant 
share of our sample stocks, collective investor behavior can be inferred 
from

at for a significant 
share of our sample stocks, collective investor behavior can be inferred 
from large-scale Wikipedia search data for individual-level stocks. 
Using Shannon transfer entropy, a model-free measure that considers 
any kind of statistical dependence between the time series of relative 
changes in Wikipedia page views and stock returns, we can infer on the 
dominant direction of the information transfer for each company's 
stock. It is possible to identify Wiki-stocks, i.e., stocks for which the 
dominant direction of the information transfer points from Wikipedia 
searches to returns. While Wiki-stocks have a lower market capitaliza­
tion on average, comparing them to the remaining stocks in our sample 
based on extreme returns and abnormal trading volume reveals that

e remaining stocks in our sample 
based on extreme returns and abnormal trading volume reveals that 
Wiki-stocks do not differ substantially from these remaining stocks. 
Thus, there have to be other channels through which Wiki-stocks attract 
the attention of potential investors. In order to express our findings in 
terms of monetary values, we design a hypothetical trading strategy 
based on Wikipedia search momentum that maps our findings to 
average portfolio returns and provides some economic interpretation 
for the transfer entropy estimates. We show that it takes time for the 
momentum effect of Wikipedia searches to manifest itself in the form of 
higher returns. This is in line with the overall notion of retail investors' 
trading patterns. 
Given the increasing data

Given the increasing data availability, future research should fur­
ther refine the link between online search data and data from social 
media platforms on the one hand and retail investor behavior on the 
other hand. This would broaden our understanding of the feedback 
loops between online sources and financial market outcomes. Most 
importantly, this relates to the question of how to classify stocks for 
which the statistical information transfer from online searches to stock 
returns dominates and, ultimately, to the question what constitutes the 
driving force behind this online search momentum.

For each of the 447 companies, we identify the page-key that is associated with the respective company's English Wikipedia page, which might 
include multiple pages per component (e.g., given different spelling, treatment of special characters, or the “redirected from”-section). For example, 
the Wikipedia page for the company American Express includes page view data for the keys “American_Express” and “American_Express_Co”, which 
are both redirected to the former key. Some other companies have special characters in their keys, leading to two different

the former key. Some other companies have special characters in their keys, leading to two different key versions. For example, 
Deere & Company, for which the keys are “Deere_%26_Co.” and “Deere_&_Co.”. Additionally, if a Wikipedia page is translated into languages other 
than English and these pages use the identical page-key, we gather that data into a second page views time series containing all views for that key. 
For example, the company 3 M has the key “3 M” in all languages.11 Accordingly, for each company, we label the page views series that is 
constructed from view counts of the English Wikipedia page EN page views, and the page views series containing view counts across all languages ALL

Abstract
We analyze the phenomenon of zombiﬁcation in Europe and show that monetary
policy alone is not its only driver. Concurring phenomena explain zombie and distressed ﬁrms’ prevalence. Using Compustat data on public ﬁrms, we ﬁnd that a
rise in short-term interest rates is associated with a decrease in zombie status, suggesting that low rates constitute a favorable environment for zombie ﬁrms; there
is no evidence of credit misallocation within the ECB’s Corporate Sector Purchase
Program; and that a decrease in inﬂation and a lower state of the business cycle is
associated with a rise in zombie prevalence.

Conclusion
There is broad agreement within the literature that there is a large variation in zombie
shares across European countries and that bank lending, especially by weakly capitalized banks, is one explanation for the allocation of capital to indebted borrowers.
However, there is very little academic research as to whether the level of interest rates,
the business cycle and recession periods can be potential factors explaining the prevalence of non-viable ﬁrms. Little is also known about the ﬁrm-speciﬁc characteristics of
non-viable ﬁrms and how zombie

two categories of ﬁrms, zombie and distressed, from eight European countries to examine the relationship between business cycle and non-viable ﬁrms’ status and understand
whether monetary policy, a highly debated, but unclear driver, can explain the incidence
of zombiﬁcation.
Our ﬁndings can be summarized as follows. We conﬁrm that zombie ﬁrms are smaller
in size, have lower proﬁtability and long-term debts and liabilities. At the same time,
we determine that speciﬁc characteristics diﬀer between zombie and distressed ﬁrms.

Literature Review
The term zombie firm appeared in reference to the U.S. Savings and Loans crisis
(S&Ls) of the 1980s and 1990s (Kane 1989) and the Japanese banking crisis of
the 1990s. In the latter historical event, Caballero, Hoshi, and Kashyap (2008)
document the phenomenon of forbearance lending, a situation in which large banks
kept the credit flowing to otherwise insolvent borrowers, also called zombie firms.
Recent studies confirm the link between weakly capitalized banks and zombie
firms (Andrews and Petroulakis 2019; Acharya et al. 2019; Schivardi, Sette, and
Tabellini 2021; Giannetti and Simonov 2013), while others document the increasing
trend, above observed, and examine

Giannetti and Simonov 2013), while others document the increasing
trend, above observed, and examine whether other channels, such as the level of
interest rates, could be a factor explaining the incidence of zombification (Banerjee

and Hofmann 2018), or examine how a competitive shock affect zombie firms in
the U.S. (Brunner, De Martiis, and Valta 2024).
The widespread existence of zombie firms can be a credit misallocation issue, where credit is allocated to companies that are not economically viable, thus
keeping them afloat for longer (Caballero, Hoshi, and Kashyap 2008; Acharya
et al. 2019; Schivardi, Sette, and Tabellini 2021). However, recently, a study by
Favara, Minoiu, and Pérez (2024) shows that U.S. banks do not engage in zombie
lending, but rather unregulated financial intermediaries do.
Furthermore, lower interest rates have been discussed as a factor fostering
the development of zombie firms, since indebted firms could become more viable
at lower rates thus reducing the pressure on zombie firms to exit

ted firms could become more viable
at lower rates thus reducing the pressure on zombie firms to exit the market or
restructure (Banerjee and Hofmann 2018). However, the literature has not found
a clear link between interest rates and the incidence of zombie firms.
Our analysis is most closely related to two strands of literature. The first,

(see, for instance, Gepp, Kumar, and Bhattacharya (2010), Chen (2011), BrezigarMasten and Masten (2012), Liang, Tsai, and Wu (2015), and Bargagli Stoffi, Riccaboni, and Rungi (2023)). Brezigar-Masten and Masten (2012) apply decision

of zombie firms. The focus of this literature is however on methodological issues.
In our paper, the interest is instead on two classes of firms, the zombie firms and
the recovered zombies and on firms in the U.S. and Europe. Our contribution to

Empirical Strategy
In this study, we develop an early warning system and we do so by considering
two prediction tasks.
On the one hand, we study zombies versus non-zombie
firms, and on the other zombies versus recovered zombie firms. While the first
task seeks to separate zombies from non-zombies, the second aims at separating
zombies that have the potential to recover from those firms that remain in the
zombie status. For both tasks, relevant variables are selected

large number of variables of the data sets that we use renders it cumbersome, if not
impossible, to analyze the features of zombie firms and select important variables
to predict the zombie status based on standard parametric models. Therefore, we
resort to machine learning algorithms that are fit for the task (Breiman 2001).

4.1
Tree-Based Models
The advantage of a decision tree is its simplicity in combination with outstanding interpretability through elegant visualization. In contrast to classic statistic
knowledge-based models, the tree finds the relevant characteristics directly from
the data without the need for assumptions.

The idea behind decision trees is to split the input space X subsequently, into
segments, where each segment decides for one class.5 Accordingly, in each section,
the outcome variable y is modeled with a different constant, e.g., a majority vote
in classification problems. The algorithm does one binary split only for a single
input feature at each iteration.
After each iteration, the decision tree repeats
the procedure in the new sub-samples until a stopping criteria is reached, thus
preventing overfitting or underfitting, by setting constraints on tree size (e.g.,
an upper bound on the depth of the tree) or performing tree pruning, another
technique that reduces the size of the tree (Khandani, Kim, and Lo 2010).
